metadata.title: Teaching quality as a dynamic system: How school support, psychological needs, and motivation interact across needs–skills configurations

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses publicly available, de-identified OECD TALIS 2024 teacher survey data for Shanghai, China (N=3976 teachers). The manuscript does not report the use of TALIS sampling/student weights or any replicate-weight scheme, nor does it name any weight variables (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or describe complex-survey variance estimation. Because the analysis is based on network estimation of partial correlations and bootstrapped stability/accuracy, the paper does not document whether weights were applied to obtain population-representative estimates. Analysts using the TALIS microdata should check the TALIS codebook for appropriate teacher sampling weights and replicate weights and apply them if the goal is inference to the target teacher population; otherwise, the reported network structure should be treated as descriptive of the analytic sample.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The study does not use plausible values because the dependent constructs are self-reported TALIS scales (teaching practices, motivation, needs, and school support), not PV-based cognitive achievement scores. Missing data handling is described as using full information maximum likelihood (FIML) with robust maximum likelihood, which is a model-based approach rather than an explicit PV framework; however, the paper does not provide a detailed missingness mechanism or an explicit imputation model specification. This means the exact effective imputation behavior cannot be fully audited from the text alone, though the authors state missingness is minimal (<1%).

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used TALIS 2024 publicly available de-identified teacher data restricted to Shanghai, China. The analytic sample includes 3976 teachers across various subjects and grade levels. Teachers were classified into three needs–performance configurations using a theory-guided continuous difference-score approach: psychological needs composite and teaching performance composite were standardized, a difference index was computed, and teachers were assigned to HNG (z ≥ +0.5 SD), BNPG (−0.5 SD < z < +0.5 SD; N=778 reported), or HPG (z ≤ −0.5 SD). Missing data were handled via robust maximum likelihood with full information maximum likelihood, with missingness reported as minimal (<1%).

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2024 (Shanghai, China) teacher survey network (no grade/domain restriction stated)
main_findings.target_variable: Teaching performance (overall network; teaching practices T1–T4)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Network edge weights (partial correlations) reported for strongest edges: T1–M1 r=0.209; T1–M3 r=-0.018; T2–A2 r=0.175; T2–S2 r=-0.023; T3–C2 r=0.243; T3–R1 r=-0.116; T4–A2 r=0.215; T4–R2 r=-0.027. Network accuracy/stability: bridge-strength CS-coefficient >0.8; non-zero edges=75/105 (density=71.43%).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2024 (Shanghai, China) teacher survey network the study leveraged digital tools self-efficacy (C2), teaching self-efficacy (M1), teaching autonomy (A2), instructional leadership (S2), and trust in school (R2) to model teaching performance (teaching practices T1–T4) as a partial-correlation network, finding that self-efficacy (M1 and C2) and autonomy (A2) were the most proximal correlates while instructional leadership (S2) and trust in school (R2) acted as distal correlates. This indicates that professional development should prioritize efficacy-building and autonomy-supportive practices, while leadership and trust may matter more indirectly through broader motivational and resource pathways, though the cross-sectional network design does not establish causal effects.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2024 (Shanghai, China) teacher survey network by needs–performance configuration (HNG/BNPG/HPG)
main_findings.target_variable: Teaching performance network structure differences across needs–performance configurations
main_findings.performance_metrics: Permutation-based network comparison: structural invariance significant across all pairs (all p<0.01). Global strength (summed absolute edge weights): 6.14 (HNG), 6.80 (BNPG), 7.00 (HPG); ΔS HNG vs BNPG=0.40 (p=.72, non-significant), ΔS HNG vs HPG=5.43 (p<.01), ΔS BNPG vs HPG=5.03 (p<.01). Edge-level examples: M2–M3 r≈0.000 (HNG), r≈0.009 (BNPG), r≈-0.044 (HPG); T2–M2 r≈-0.016 (HNG), r≈0.020 (BNPG), r≈0.000 (HPG); T3–T1 r≈0.082 (HNG), r≈0.018 (BNPG), r≈-0.008 (HPG).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2024 (Shanghai, China) teacher survey network the study leveraged digital tools self-efficacy (C2), teaching self-efficacy (M1), distributed leadership (S1), instructional leadership (S2), and career motivations (M2) to compare teaching-performance network structures across needs–performance configurations, finding that network structure differed significantly across groups (permutation tests all p<0.01) with global strength increasing as needs decreased relative to performance (6.14→6.80→7.00) and multiple edge weights reversing or weakening across configurations. This indicates that teacher support and professional development should be alignment-sensitive—targeting different leverage points depending on whether teachers report high needs/low performance versus balanced or high performance/low needs—while recognizing that these configuration differences are exploratory and based on cross-sectional self-reports.

data.outcome_summary: This study uses OECD TALIS 2024 teacher survey data restricted to Shanghai, China (N=3976 teachers) to model teaching performance as a dynamic, multi-dimensional network of TALIS “teaching practices” (T1–T4) alongside school support, basic psychological needs, and motivation. Rather than training a predictive ML model, the authors estimate cross-factor networks using partial correlations and compare network structure across three needs–performance configurations (HNG, BNPG, HPG) derived from standardized difference scores. The overall network shows self-efficacy as proximal: the strongest edges include T1–M1 (r=0.209) and T3–C2 (r=0.243), while instructional leadership (S2) and trust in school (R2) function as distal correlates. Network comparisons indicate significant structural invariance across configurations (all p<0.01) and configuration-specific edge reversals (e.g., M2–M3: ~0.000, 0.009, −0.044). Limitations include cross-sectional design (no temporal ordering/causality), self-report measurement, and no documented use of TALIS sampling weights.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This paper is not an empirical predictive ML study: it uses network analysis (partial correlations, centrality, and permutation-based network comparisons) to examine interrelations and configuration-specific structural differences. Consequently, no supervised ML algorithms are trained or evaluated, so ml_techniques.all_techniques is empty and ml_techniques.primary is null. The main findings therefore report network edge weights and network-structure comparison statistics rather than ML predictive performance (e.g., accuracy/AUC).
